raw_evidence.label: Background: Fell vs. Found — the central distinction
raw_evidence.content: Every entry in the Meteoritical Bulletin is tagged either 'Fell' or 'Found'. A Fell is a meteorite whose descent was actually observed by a human witness — somebody saw the fireball, heard the sonic boom, and the recovered rock could be matched to that event. A Find is a meteorite that was located on the ground without anyone seeing it land. This is not a minor distinction: only about 1,107 of the 45,716 rows in this dataset are Fells, just 2.4%. Fells dominate the historical record before about 1900 because no large-scale meteorite-hunting program existed; Finds explode after 1969 when systematic recovery on Antarctic blue ice began. Almost everything else interesting about this dataset — geography, mass distribution, year coverage — is downstream of this one selection rule. The Meteoritical Society's glossary defines 'fall' as 'a meteorite that was seen while it fell to Earth and found', and 'find' as 'a meteorite that was found without seeing it fall'.

raw_evidence.label: Background: How many meteorites actually hit Earth per year
raw_evidence.content: The reason Fells are so rare is not that meteorites are rare — it is that witnessing one is. Researchers estimate roughly 6,100 meteorite falls per year over the entire Earth, of which about 1,800 land on land rather than ocean. The number actually recovered and added to the Meteoritical Bulletin as observed falls is closer to 6–10 per year historically (about 7.9 per year averaged over 2007–2018), rising past 10 per year since 2020 as dashcams, doorbell cameras, and amateur fireball networks expand. So roughly 99.99% of all rocks that land on dry ground vanish into rivers, forests, and farmland without being identified.

raw_evidence.label: Fell vs Found — 2.42% of all named meteorites were ever seen falling
raw_evidence.content: The headline split of the catalogue: 1,107 rows (2.42%) are Fells where a human witnessed the descent; 44,608 (97.58%) are Founds where the rock was recognised on the ground at some unknown later date. This is the single biggest selection effect in the dataset. The Detective's external benchmark — roughly 1,800 land-falls per year, of which only about 7–10 become observed-fall records — implies a true witnessing rate of well under 1%, consistent with what the dataset shows.

print(f"Found pct = {vc.get('Found',0)/total*100:.2f}%")

raw_evidence.label: Dataset profile
raw_evidence.content: The dataset contains 45,716 rows and 10 columns, with one row per officially-named meteorite. Of these, 1,107 (2.42%) are observed Fells and 44,609 (97.58%) are post-recovery Finds; 45,641 are Valid and only 75 are Relict (heavily weathered). The recclass column has 466 distinct values, the year column ranges from 860 to 2,101 (one typo) with 291 nulls, and mass(g) ranges from 0 to 60,000,000 with 131 nulls. Coordinates are missing for 7,315 rows (16.0%).

print(f"columns={list(df.columns)}")

print(f"valid_nametype={int((df['nametype']=='Valid').sum()):,}  relict={int((df['nametype']=='Relict').sum()):,}")
print(f"distinct_recclass={df['recclass'].nunique()}")
print(f"distinct_names={df['name'].nunique()}")
print(f"year_min={df['year'].min()}  year_max={df['year'].max()}  null_years={int(df['year'].isna().sum())}")
print(f"mass_g_min={df['mass (g)'].min()}  mass_g_max={df['mass (g)'].max():.0f}  null_mass={int(df['mass (g)'].isna().sum())}")
print(f"missing_coords={int(df['reclat'].isna().sum()):,}  ({df['reclat'].isna().mean()*100:.1f}%)")

raw_evidence.label: Background: Fell vs. Found — the central distinction
raw_evidence.content: Every entry in the Meteoritical Bulletin is tagged either 'Fell' or 'Found'. A Fell is a meteorite whose descent was actually observed by a human witness — somebody saw the fireball, heard the sonic boom, and the recovered rock could be matched to that event. A Find is a meteorite that was located on the ground without anyone seeing it land. This is not a minor distinction: only about 1,107 of the 45,716 rows in this dataset are Fells, just 2.4%. Fells dominate the historical record before about 1900 because no large-scale meteorite-hunting program existed; Finds explode after 1969 when systematic recovery on Antarctic blue ice began. Almost everything else interesting about this dataset — geography, mass distribution, year coverage — is downstream of this one selection rule. The Meteoritical Society's glossary defines 'fall' as 'a meteorite that was seen while it fell to Earth and found', and 'find' as 'a meteorite that was found without seeing it fall'.

raw_evidence.label: Background: How many meteorites actually hit Earth per year
raw_evidence.content: The reason Fells are so rare is not that meteorites are rare — it is that witnessing one is. Researchers estimate roughly 6,100 meteorite falls per year over the entire Earth, of which about 1,800 land on land rather than ocean. The number actually recovered and added to the Meteoritical Bulletin as observed falls is closer to 6–10 per year historically (about 7.9 per year averaged over 2007–2018), rising past 10 per year since 2020 as dashcams, doorbell cameras, and amateur fireball networks expand. So roughly 99.99% of all rocks that land on dry ground vanish into rivers, forests, and farmland without being identified.

Source: FAQs — ANSMET (Antarctic Search for Meteorites) (https://caslabs.case.edu/ansmet/faqs/) Facts: Teams of 4–10 explorers live for 5–7 weeks on the ice field; Snowmobiles spaced 30 m apart scan blue ice for meteorites Source: ANSMET — Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANSMET) Facts: As of end-2022, ANSMET had recovered slightly more than 23,000 specimens

raw_evidence.label: Background: Where Finds come from — Antarctic blue ice
raw_evidence.content: The 44,609 Finds in the dataset are wildly geographically skewed, and the reason is operational, not physical: nearly all meteorites land more or less uniformly across the planet, but they only stand out in two places — Antarctic blue ice and hot deserts. The Antarctic Search for Meteorites (ANSMET), run from Case Western Reserve University since 1976, dispatches teams of 4–10 scientists for 5–7 weeks each austral summer; they ride snowmobiles spaced 30 m apart across blue-ice areas. Blue ice forms where katabatic winds blowing off the polar plateau ablate snow faster than it falls, exposing dense, blue-tinted ice in which meteorites accumulated over hundreds of thousands of years are scoured back to the surface. As of late 2022 ANSMET alone had recovered slightly more than 23,000 specimens; combined with Japanese (NIPR) and Chinese programs, well over half of all officially-named meteorites in this snapshot are from Antarctica. None of these are Fells: the rocks have been entombed in ice for millennia.

Before 1700 the record is almost entirely sparse Fells from Europe and East Asia (Nogata 860, Narni 920, Elbogen 1399, Ensisheim 1491). Founds stay below 100/decade until the 1960s, then explode: 4,909 in the 1970s, 6,766 in the 1980s, 11,563 in the 1990s, 17,698 in the 2000s. The 2010s entry (1,963) reflects the dataset being frozen ~2013.

raw_evidence.label: Background: Where Finds come from — Antarctic blue ice
raw_evidence.content: The 44,609 Finds in the dataset are wildly geographically skewed, and the reason is operational, not physical: nearly all meteorites land more or less uniformly across the planet, but they only stand out in two places — Antarctic blue ice and hot deserts. The Antarctic Search for Meteorites (ANSMET), run from Case Western Reserve University since 1976, dispatches teams of 4–10 scientists for 5–7 weeks each austral summer; they ride snowmobiles spaced 30 m apart across blue-ice areas. Blue ice forms where katabatic winds blowing off the polar plateau ablate snow faster than it falls, exposing dense, blue-tinted ice in which meteorites accumulated over hundreds of thousands of years are scoured back to the surface. As of late 2022 ANSMET alone had recovered slightly more than 23,000 specimens; combined with Japanese (NIPR) and Chinese programs, well over half of all officially-named meteorites in this snapshot are from Antarctica. None of these are Fells: the rocks have been entombed in ice for millennia.

raw_evidence.label: Decade-by-decade Fell vs Found counts (860-2010s)
raw_evidence.content: Decade-resolved counts trace the catalogue's growth. Before 1700 the record is almost entirely sparse Fells from Europe and East Asia (Nogata 860, Narni 920, Elbogen 1399, Ensisheim 1491). Fells grow modestly through the 1800s into a steady 50-90/decade in the 20th century. Founds stay below 100/decade until the 1960s, then explode: 4,909 in the 1970s, 6,766 in the 1980s, 11,563 in the 1990s, 17,698 in the 2000s. The 2010s entry (1,963) reflects the dataset being frozen ~2013.
raw_evidence.code:
print("\n=== ana_06 ===")
d = df.dropna(subset=['year']).copy()
d['decade'] = (d['year'] // 10 * 10).astype(int)
piv = d.pivot_table(index='decade', columns='fall', values='id', aggfunc='count', fill_value=0)
piv = piv.reindex(columns=['Fell','Found'], fill_value=0)
piv['Total'] = piv.sum(axis=1)
piv = piv[piv['Total'] > 0]
print(piv.to_string())

raw_evidence.label: Antarctica accounts for 59% of all geocoded Founds — and 0% of Fells
raw_evidence.content: Splitting at latitude -60° (the Antarctic Circle plus a buffer): 22,099 rows lie in Antarctica, every single one a Found, and zero Fells. Outside Antarctica, the catalogue is 1,097 Fells and 15,204 Founds — a much more balanced 6.73% Fell rate. So Antarctica alone supplies 59.2% of every geocoded Find in the dataset, and contributes nothing to the Fell record. No one is standing under Antarctic skies to watch a meteorite fall; the ice does the collecting passively, over millennia (det_04).
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_14: Antarctic vs rest of world ---
print("\n=== ana_14 ===")
geo['region'] = np.where(geo['reclat'] < -60, 'Antarctica (lat<-60)', 'Rest of world')
piv = geo.pivot_table(index='region', columns='fall', values='id', aggfunc='count', fill_value=0)
piv['Total'] = piv.sum(axis=1)
piv['%Fell'] = (piv.get('Fell',0) / piv['Total'] * 100).round(3)
print(piv.to_string())

raw_evidence.label: Hot-desert recovery hotspots: Sahara, Arabia, US SW, Australia, Atacama
raw_evidence.content: Stripping out Antarctica and the rest-of-world residual, the dataset's other big concentrations are all desert recovery zones. The Arabian peninsula and Oman supply 3,154 meteorites, the Sahara/Sahel 2,414, the US south-west deserts 1,063, the Australian outback 540, and the Atacama in Chile 415. All five have %Fell rates well below the rest-of-world figure: people are out there hunting, not happening to be present at a fall. The famous Hot-Desert Meteorites (HDM) of the post-2000 boom are visible in the data as these latitude-banded blocks.
raw_evidence.code:
print(f"Share of all geocoded Fells that are in Antarctica: {((geo['fall']=='Fell')  & (geo['reclat']<-60)).sum() / max(1,(geo['fall']=='Fell').sum()) * 100:.2f}%")

# --- ana_15: Coarse region buckets (Antarctica vs hot-desert belts vs rest) ---
print("\n=== ana_15 ===")
def region(row):
    lat, lon = row['reclat'], row['reclong']
    if lat < -60: return "Antarctica"
    # Sahara/Sahel: lat 15..32, lon -17..40
    if 15 <= lat <= 32 and -17 <= lon <= 40: return "Sahara/Sahel"
    # Arabian + Oman: lat 16..28, lon 35..60
    if 16 <= lat <= 28 and 35 <= lon <= 60: return "Arabia/Oman"
    # Atacama: lat -30..-15, lon -72..-65
    if -30 <= lat <= -15 and -72 <= lon <= -65: return "Atacama (Chile)"
    # Australia outback: lat -32..-18, lon 115..150
    if -32 <= lat <= -18 and 115 <= lon <= 150: return "Australian outback"
    # Western US (deserts): lat 30..42, lon -120..-100
    if 30 <= lat <= 42 and -120 <= lon <= -100: return "US SW deserts"
    return "Rest of world"

geo['region2'] = geo.apply(region, axis=1)
piv = geo.pivot_table(index='region2', columns='fall', values='id', aggfunc='count', fill_value=0)
piv['Total'] = piv.sum(axis=1)
piv['%Fell'] = (piv.get('Fell',0) / piv['Total'] * 100).round(2)

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: Why the top five are all irons
raw_evidence.content: Sort the dataset by mass descending and you get Hoba (Namibia, 60 t), Cape York/Ahnighito (Greenland, ~31 t — actually a fragment of a larger fall), Campo del Cielo/Gancedo (Argentina, ~31 t), Canyon Diablo (Arizona, ~30 t total recovered), and Armanty (Xinjiang, 28 t). Every one is an iron meteorite. This is not random: irons survive both atmospheric entry and weathering far better than stony meteorites. Ordinary chondrites — L6, H5, LL5 — make up about 87% of all observed falls (and the bulk of this dataset by row count), but they crumble. An iron block sits intact for tens of thousands of years; a chondrite the same size shatters into pebbles and rusts away. So the mass-ranked top of the table is not a sample of what hits Earth — it is a sample of what is hard enough to still be found.

raw_evidence.label: Mass distribution is log-normal over 10 orders of magnitude
raw_evidence.content: Meteorite masses span from sub-gram chips to the 60-tonne Hoba — ten orders of magnitude on a linear axis. m = df['mass (g)'].dropna()
m = m[m > 0]
bins = [1e-3, 1, 10, 100, 1e3, 1e4, 1e5, 1e6, 1e7, 1e8]

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: Hoba, the 60-ton single-piece meteorite
raw_evidence.content: The single heaviest row in the dataset is the Hoba meteorite, a 60,000,000-gram (60-ton) iron block in Otjozondjupa, Namibia (19.583°S, 17.917°E). It is so heavy that, since being discovered by a farmer ploughing a field in 1920, no one has ever moved it — it was declared a Namibian national monument in 1955 and is still sitting where it landed less than 80,000 years ago. Composition: roughly 84% iron, 16% nickel, trace cobalt; classified as an ataxite iron (IVB chemical class). The fact that the largest known meteorite is iron is not an accident — see det_07. Hoba's mass alone is large enough that whatever chart shows mass on a linear axis becomes useless; this row is the reason every analyst defaults to a log scale on mass(g).

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: Cape York and the Inughuit iron trade
raw_evidence.content: The Cape York / Innaanganeq meteorite (Greenland, ~58 t across eight fragments) entered the scientific literature in 1894 when Robert Peary, guided by Inughuit Inuit, reached the site and spent three years removing the three largest pieces, including the 30.88-ton Ahnighito ('the Tent'). He sold them to the American Museum of Natural History in New York for $40,000. But the Inughuit had been quarrying iron tools from these blocks for centuries by cold-forging — hammering chunks with stones — and trading them across the Arctic. The Cape York rows in the dataset are simultaneously a top-five-heaviest entry, a colonial-collection story, and one of the very few documented cases of a pre-industrial society sourcing iron exclusively from meteorites.

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: Campo del Cielo, a 4,500-year-old crater field
raw_evidence.content: Campo del Cielo ('Field of Heaven' in Spanish, 'Piguem Nonralta' to the indigenous Mocoví) is a 4,200–4,700-year-old impact field in Argentina's Chaco and Santiago del Estero provinces — at least 26 craters scattered over 18.5 by 3 km. About 100 tonnes of iron fragments have been recovered, the most ever from a single fall event; the two largest, Gancedo (30.8 t, found 2016) and El Chaco (28.8 t, found 1969), are themselves global top-five meteorites. The Spanish colonial governor first commissioned an expedition in 1576 after hearing indigenous accounts; native peoples had been using the iron for weapons long before that. This makes Campo del Cielo the closest the dataset comes to a 'meteor strike caught on Earth's geological video tape' — old enough to predate writing in the region, fresh enough that the craters still exist.

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: Hoba, the 60-ton single-piece meteorite
raw_evidence.content: The single heaviest row in the dataset is the Hoba meteorite, a 60,000,000-gram (60-ton) iron block in Otjozondjupa, Namibia (19.583°S, 17.917°E). It is so heavy that, since being discovered by a farmer ploughing a field in 1920, no one has ever moved it — it was declared a Namibian national monument in 1955 and is still sitting where it landed less than 80,000 years ago. Composition: roughly 84% iron, 16% nickel, trace cobalt; classified as an ataxite iron (IVB chemical class). The fact that the largest known meteorite is iron is not an accident — see det_07. raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: Why the top five are all irons
raw_evidence.content: Sort the dataset by mass descending and you get Hoba (Namibia, 60 t), Cape York/Ahnighito (Greenland, ~31 t — actually a fragment of a larger fall), Campo del Cielo/Gancedo (Argentina, ~31 t), Canyon Diablo (Arizona, ~30 t total recovered), and Armanty (Xinjiang, 28 t). Every one is an iron meteorite. This is not random: irons survive both atmospheric entry and weathering far better than stony meteorites. Ordinary chondrites — L6, H5, LL5 — make up about 87% of all observed falls (and the bulk of this dataset by row count), but they crumble. An iron block sits intact for tens of thousands of years; a chondrite the same size shatters into pebbles and rusts away. So the mass-ranked top of the table is not a sample of what hits Earth — it is a sample of what is hard enough to still be found.

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: Cape York and the Inughuit iron trade
raw_evidence.content: The Cape York / Innaanganeq meteorite (Greenland, ~58 t across eight fragments) entered the scientific literature in 1894 when Robert Peary, guided by Inughuit Inuit, reached the site and spent three years removing the three largest pieces, including the 30.88-ton Ahnighito ('the Tent'). He sold them to the American Museum of Natural History in New York for $40,000. But the Inughuit had been quarrying iron tools from these blocks for centuries by cold-forging — hammering chunks with stones — and trading them across the Arctic. The Cape York rows in the dataset are simultaneously a top-five-heaviest entry, a colonial-collection story, and one of the very few documented cases of a pre-industrial society sourcing iron exclusively from meteorites.

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: Campo del Cielo, a 4,500-year-old crater field
raw_evidence.content: Campo del Cielo ('Field of Heaven' in Spanish, 'Piguem Nonralta' to the indigenous Mocoví) is a 4,200–4,700-year-old impact field in Argentina's Chaco and Santiago del Estero provinces — at least 26 craters scattered over 18.5 by 3 km. About 100 tonnes of iron fragments have been recovered, the most ever from a single fall event; the two largest, Gancedo (30.8 t, found 2016) and El Chaco (28.8 t, found 1969), are themselves global top-five meteorites. The Spanish colonial governor first commissioned an expedition in 1576 after hearing indigenous accounts; native peoples had been using the iron for weapons long before that. This makes Campo del Cielo the closest the dataset comes to a 'meteor strike caught on Earth's geological video tape' — old enough to predate writing in the region, fresh enough that the craters still exist.

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: Why the top five are all irons
raw_evidence.content: Sort the dataset by mass descending and you get Hoba (Namibia, 60 t), Cape York/Ahnighito (Greenland, ~31 t — actually a fragment of a larger fall), Campo del Cielo/Gancedo (Argentina, ~31 t), Canyon Diablo (Arizona, ~30 t total recovered), and Armanty (Xinjiang, 28 t). Every one is an iron meteorite. This is not random: irons survive both atmospheric entry and weathering far better than stony meteorites. Ordinary chondrites — L6, H5, LL5 — make up about 87% of all observed falls (and the bulk of this dataset by row count), but they crumble. An iron block sits intact for tens of thousands of years; a chondrite the same size shatters into pebbles and rusts away. So the mass-ranked top of the table is not a sample of what hits Earth — it is a sample of what is hard enough to still be found.

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: Cape York and the Inughuit iron trade
raw_evidence.content: The Cape York / Innaanganeq meteorite (Greenland, ~58 t across eight fragments) entered the scientific literature in 1894 when Robert Peary, guided by Inughuit Inuit, reached the site and spent three years removing the three largest pieces, including the 30.88-ton Ahnighito ('the Tent'). He sold them to the American Museum of Natural History in New York for $40,000. But the Inughuit had been quarrying iron tools from these blocks for centuries by cold-forging — hammering chunks with stones — and trading them across the Arctic. The Cape York rows in the dataset are simultaneously a top-five-heaviest entry, a colonial-collection story, and one of the very few documented cases of a pre-industrial society sourcing iron exclusively from meteorites.

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: Campo del Cielo, a 4,500-year-old crater field
raw_evidence.content: Campo del Cielo ('Field of Heaven' in Spanish, 'Piguem Nonralta' to the indigenous Mocoví) is a 4,200–4,700-year-old impact field in Argentina's Chaco and Santiago del Estero provinces — at least 26 craters scattered over 18.5 by 3 km. About 100 tonnes of iron fragments have been recovered, the most ever from a single fall event; the two largest, Gancedo (30.8 t, found 2016) and El Chaco (28.8 t, found 1969), are themselves global top-five meteorites. The Spanish colonial governor first commissioned an expedition in 1576 after hearing indigenous accounts; native peoples had been using the iron for weapons long before that. This makes Campo del Cielo the closest the dataset comes to a 'meteor strike caught on Earth's geological video tape' — old enough to predate writing in the region, fresh enough that the craters still exist.

Chondrites that big rarely survive any of those filters.

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: Why the top five are all irons
raw_evidence.content: Sort the dataset by mass descending and you get Hoba (Namibia, 60 t), Cape York/Ahnighito (Greenland, ~31 t — actually a fragment of a larger fall), Campo del Cielo/Gancedo (Argentina, ~31 t), Canyon Diablo (Arizona, ~30 t total recovered), and Armanty (Xinjiang, 28 t). An iron block sits intact for tens of thousands of years; a chondrite the same size shatters into pebbles and rusts away. So the mass-ranked top of the table is not a sample of what hits Earth — it is a sample of what is hard enough to still be found.

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: Cape York and the Inughuit iron trade
raw_evidence.content: The Cape York / Innaanganeq meteorite (Greenland, ~58 t across eight fragments) entered the scientific literature in 1894 when Robert Peary, guided by Inughuit Inuit, reached the site and spent three years removing the three largest pieces, including the 30.88-ton Ahnighito ('the Tent'). He sold them to the American Museum of Natural History in New York for $40,000. But the Inughuit had been quarrying iron tools from these blocks for centuries by cold-forging — hammering chunks with stones — and trading them across the Arctic. The Cape York rows in the dataset are simultaneously a top-five-heaviest entry, a colonial-collection story, and one of the very few documented cases of a pre-industrial society sourcing iron exclusively from meteorites.

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: Hoba, the 60-ton single-piece meteorite
raw_evidence.content: The single heaviest row in the dataset is the Hoba meteorite, a 60,000,000-gram (60-ton) iron block in Otjozondjupa, Namibia (19.583°S, 17.917°E). It is so heavy that, since being discovered by a farmer ploughing a field in 1920, no one has ever moved it — it was declared a Namibian national monument in 1955 and is still sitting where it landed less than 80,000 years ago. Composition: roughly 84% iron, 16% nickel, trace cobalt; classified as an ataxite iron (IVB chemical class). The fact that the largest known meteorite is iron is not an accident — see det_07. Hoba's mass alone is large enough that whatever chart shows mass on a linear axis becomes useless; this row is the reason every analyst defaults to a log scale on mass(g).

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: Why the top five are all irons
raw_evidence.content: Sort the dataset by mass descending and you get Hoba (Namibia, 60 t), Cape York/Ahnighito (Greenland, ~31 t — actually a fragment of a larger fall), Campo del Cielo/Gancedo (Argentina, ~31 t), Canyon Diablo (Arizona, ~30 t total recovered), and Armanty (Xinjiang, 28 t). Every one is an iron meteorite. This is not random: irons survive both atmospheric entry and weathering far better than stony meteorites. Ordinary chondrites — L6, H5, LL5 — make up about 87% of all observed falls (and the bulk of this dataset by row count), but they crumble. An iron block sits intact for tens of thousands of years; a chondrite the same size shatters into pebbles and rusts away. So the mass-ranked top of the table is not a sample of what hits Earth — it is a sample of what is hard enough to still be found.

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: Cape York and the Inughuit iron trade
raw_evidence.content: The Cape York / Innaanganeq meteorite (Greenland, ~58 t across eight fragments) entered the scientific literature in 1894 when Robert Peary, guided by Inughuit Inuit, reached the site and spent three years removing the three largest pieces, including the 30.88-ton Ahnighito ('the Tent'). He sold them to the American Museum of Natural History in New York for $40,000. But the Inughuit had been quarrying iron tools from these blocks for centuries by cold-forging — hammering chunks with stones — and trading them across the Arctic. The Cape York rows in the dataset are simultaneously a top-five-heaviest entry, a colonial-collection story, and one of the very few documented cases of a pre-industrial society sourcing iron exclusively from meteorites.

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: Campo del Cielo, a 4,500-year-old crater field
raw_evidence.content: Campo del Cielo ('Field of Heaven' in Spanish, 'Piguem Nonralta' to the indigenous Mocoví) is a 4,200–4,700-year-old impact field in Argentina's Chaco and Santiago del Estero provinces — at least 26 craters scattered over 18.5 by 3 km. About 100 tonnes of iron fragments have been recovered, the most ever from a single fall event; the two largest, Gancedo (30.8 t, found 2016) and El Chaco (28.8 t, found 1969), are themselves global top-five meteorites. The Spanish colonial governor first commissioned an expedition in 1576 after hearing indigenous accounts; native peoples had been using the iron for weapons long before that. This makes Campo del Cielo the closest the dataset comes to a 'meteor strike caught on Earth's geological video tape' — old enough to predate writing in the region, fresh enough that the craters still exist.

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: Hoba, the 60-ton single-piece meteorite
raw_evidence.content: The single heaviest row in the dataset is the Hoba meteorite, a 60,000,000-gram (60-ton) iron block in Otjozondjupa, Namibia (19.583°S, 17.917°E). It is so heavy that, since being discovered by a farmer ploughing a field in 1920, no one has ever moved it — it was declared a Namibian national monument in 1955 and is still sitting where it landed less than 80,000 years ago. Hoba's mass alone is large enough that whatever chart shows mass on a linear axis becomes useless; this row is the reason every analyst defaults to a log scale on mass(g).

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: Why the top five are all irons
raw_evidence.content: Sort the dataset by mass descending and you get Hoba (Namibia, 60 t), Cape York/Ahnighito (Greenland, ~31 t — actually a fragment of a larger fall), Campo del Cielo/Gancedo (Argentina, ~31 t), Canyon Diablo (Arizona, ~30 t total recovered), and Armanty (Xinjiang, 28 t). Every one is an iron meteorite. This is not random: irons survive both atmospheric entry and weathering far better than stony meteorites. Ordinary chondrites — L6, H5, LL5 — make up about 87% of all observed falls (and the bulk of this dataset by row count), but they crumble. An iron block sits intact for tens of thousands of years; a chondrite the same size shatters into pebbles and rusts away. So the mass-ranked top of the table is not a sample of what hits Earth — it is a sample of what is hard enough to still be found.

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: Hoba, the 60-ton single-piece meteorite
raw_evidence.content: The single heaviest row in the dataset is the Hoba meteorite, a 60,000,000-gram (60-ton) iron block in Otjozondjupa, Namibia (19.583°S, 17.917°E). It is so heavy that, since being discovered by a farmer ploughing a field in 1920, no one has ever moved it — it was declared a Namibian national monument in 1955 and is still sitting where it landed less than 80,000 years ago. Composition: roughly 84% iron, 16% nickel, trace cobalt; classified as an ataxite iron (IVB chemical class). The fact that the largest known meteorite is iron is not an accident — see det_07. Hoba's mass alone is large enough that whatever chart shows mass on a linear axis becomes useless; this row is the reason every analyst defaults to a log scale on mass(g).

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: Why the top five are all irons
raw_evidence.content: Sort the dataset by mass descending and you get Hoba (Namibia, 60 t), Cape York/Ahnighito (Greenland, ~31 t — actually a fragment of a larger fall), Campo del Cielo/Gancedo (Argentina, ~31 t), Canyon Diablo (Arizona, ~30 t total recovered), and Armanty (Xinjiang, 28 t). Every one is an iron meteorite. This is not random: irons survive both atmospheric entry and weathering far better than stony meteorites. Ordinary chondrites — L6, H5, LL5 — make up about 87% of all observed falls (and the bulk of this dataset by row count), but they crumble. An iron block sits intact for tens of thousands of years; a chondrite the same size shatters into pebbles and rusts away. So the mass-ranked top of the table is not a sample of what hits Earth — it is a sample of what is hard enough to still be found.

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: Cape York and the Inughuit iron trade
raw_evidence.content: The Cape York / Innaanganeq meteorite (Greenland, ~58 t across eight fragments) entered the scientific literature in 1894 when Robert Peary, guided by Inughuit Inuit, reached the site and spent three years removing the three largest pieces, including the 30.88-ton Ahnighito ('the Tent'). He sold them to the American Museum of Natural History in New York for $40,000. But the Inughuit had been quarrying iron tools from these blocks for centuries by cold-forging — hammering chunks with stones — and trading them across the Arctic. The Cape York rows in the dataset are simultaneously a top-five-heaviest entry, a colonial-collection story, and one of the very few documented cases of a pre-industrial society sourcing iron exclusively from meteorites.

raw_evidence.label: Background: Composition classes the analyst will see
raw_evidence.content: The recclass column has 466 distinct values, but they cluster into a few families. Stony meteorites are by far the most common: ordinary chondrites make up about 87% of all known meteorites and are split into H (high total iron), L (low total iron), and LL (low total iron + low metal) groups, each followed by a petrologic type 3–6 indicating how thermally metamorphosed they are (3 = pristine chondrules visible, 6 = recrystallised). So an 'L6' is a low-iron ordinary chondrite that has been heated almost to melting on its parent body; an 'H5' is a high-iron chondrite somewhat less metamorphosed. Then there are achondrites (differentiated stony — Howardites, Eucrites, Diogenites, etc.), iron meteorites (split into structural classes like octahedrite and ataxite, plus chemical groups IAB, IIIAB, IVA, IVB), and stony-irons (Pallasites, Mesosiderites). For the blog, the headline number is: when you sort the dataset by row count, ordinary chondrites dominate; sort by mass, and irons rule.

raw_evidence.label: Class families: ordinary chondrites are 87% of rows
raw_evidence.content: Collapsing the 466 distinct recclass strings into composition families gives a clean Pareto: Ordinary chondrites dominate at 86.96% (39,756 rows), followed by Carbonaceous chondrites at 3.50% (1,602), HED achondrites at 2.59% (1,186), Iron meteorites at just 2.34% (1,069), and a long tail of enstatite/primitive achondrites/stony-irons/lunar/Martian under 1.5% each. So irons — which dominate the heavy tail (ana_09) — are barely 1 in 43 rows by count. The Detective's '87% ordinary chondrite' benchmark from the literature lines up almost exactly with this dataset's 86.96%.
raw_evidence.code:
df['family'] = df['recclass'].apply(family)
fam_counts = df['family'].value_counts()
print(fam_counts.to_string())
total = fam_counts.sum()
print("\nPercentages:")
print((fam_counts / total * 100).round(2).to_string())

# --- ana_11: Median mass by family ---
print("\n=== ana_11 ===")
mm = df.dropna(subset=['mass (g)']).copy()
mm = mm[mm['mass (g)'] > 0]
grp = mm.groupby('family')['mass (g)'].agg(['count','median','mean'])
grp['median'] = grp['median'].round(2)
grp['mean'] = grp['mean'].round(2)

raw_evidence.label: Class families: ordinary chondrites are 87% of rows
raw_evidence.content: Collapsing the 466 distinct recclass strings into composition families gives a clean Pareto: Ordinary chondrites dominate at 86.96% (39,756 rows), followed by Carbonaceous chondrites at 3.50% (1,602), HED achondrites at 2.59% (1,186), Iron meteorites at just 2.34% (1,069), and a long tail of enstatite/primitive achondrites/stony-irons/lunar/Martian under 1.5% each. So irons — which dominate the heavy tail (ana_09) — are barely 1 in 43 rows by count. The Detective's '87% ordinary chondrite' benchmark from the literature lines up almost exactly with this dataset's 86.96%.
raw_evidence.code:
df['family'] = df['recclass'].apply(family)
fam_counts = df['family'].value_counts()
print(fam_counts.to_string())
total = fam_counts.sum()
print("\nPercentages:")
print((fam_counts / total * 100).round(2).to_string())

# --- ana_11: Median mass by family ---
print("\n=== ana_11 ===")
mm = df.dropna(subset=['mass (g)']).copy()
mm = mm[mm['mass (g)'] > 0]
grp = mm.groupby('family')['mass (g)'].agg(['count','median','mean'])
grp['median'] = grp['median'].round(2)
grp['mean'] = grp['mean'].round(2)

raw_evidence.label: Background: Composition classes the analyst will see
raw_evidence.content: The recclass column has 466 distinct values, but they cluster into a few families. Stony meteorites are by far the most common: ordinary chondrites make up about 87% of all known meteorites and are split into H (high total iron), L (low total iron), and LL (low total iron + low metal) groups, each followed by a petrologic type 3–6 indicating how thermally metamorphosed they are (3 = pristine chondrules visible, 6 = recrystallised). So an 'L6' is a low-iron ordinary chondrite that has been heated almost to melting on its parent body; an 'H5' is a high-iron chondrite somewhat less metamorphosed. Then there are achondrites (differentiated stony — Howardites, Eucrites, Diogenites, etc.), iron meteorites (split into structural classes like octahedrite and ataxite, plus chemical groups IAB, IIIAB, IVA, IVB), and stony-irons (Pallasites, Mesosiderites). For the blog, the headline number is: when you sort the dataset by row count, ordinary chondrites dominate; sort by mass, and irons rule.

raw_evidence.label: Iron meteorites are ~350x heavier than ordinary chondrites at the median
raw_evidence.content: Median masses by family lay bare the count/mass inversion. Iron meteorites have a median mass of 10,000 g (10 kg) and a mean of nearly half a tonne; ordinary chondrites have a median of 28.5 g and a mean of 1.5 kg. Stony-irons sit in between at 496 g median. The lightest typical family is Enstatite chondrites at just 8.4 g median. So even though irons are only 2.3% of the catalogue by row, on a mass-weighted basis they massively outweigh the chondrites.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_12: Family by fall (count) ---
print("\n=== ana_12 ===")
piv = df.pivot_table(index='family', columns='fall', values='id', aggfunc='count', fill_value=0)
piv['Total'] = piv.sum(axis=1)
piv['%Fell'] = (piv.get('Fell',0) / piv['Total'] * 100).round(2)
piv = piv.sort_values('Total', ascending=False)
print(piv.to_string())

Source: FAQs — ANSMET (Antarctic Search for Meteorites) (https://caslabs.case.edu/ansmet/faqs/) Facts: Teams of 4–10 explorers live for 5–7 weeks on the ice field; Snowmobiles spaced 30 m apart scan blue ice for meteorites Source: ANSMET — Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANSMET) Facts: As of end-2022, ANSMET had recovered slightly more than 23,000 specimens

raw_evidence.label: Background: Where Finds come from — Antarctic blue ice
raw_evidence.content: The 44,609 Finds in the dataset are wildly geographically skewed, and the reason is operational, not physical: nearly all meteorites land more or less uniformly across the planet, but they only stand out in two places — Antarctic blue ice and hot deserts. The Antarctic Search for Meteorites (ANSMET), run from Case Western Reserve University since 1976, dispatches teams of 4–10 scientists for 5–7 weeks each austral summer; they ride snowmobiles spaced 30 m apart across blue-ice areas. Blue ice forms where katabatic winds blowing off the polar plateau ablate snow faster than it falls, exposing dense, blue-tinted ice in which meteorites accumulated over hundreds of thousands of years are scoured back to the surface. As of late 2022 ANSMET alone had recovered slightly more than 23,000 specimens; combined with Japanese (NIPR) and Chinese programs, well over half of all officially-named meteorites in this snapshot are from Antarctica. None of these are Fells: the rocks have been entombed in ice for millennia.

raw_evidence.label: Antarctic decade share: from 0% before 1969 to 93% in the 1980s, falling back as deserts took over
raw_evidence.content: Splitting the geocoded post-1820 record by decade and Antarctica vs Rest-of-World shows three distinct eras. Pre-1969: zero Antarctic finds (one outlier from 1912 — likely Shackleton-era). 1970s-1980s: Antarctica dominates absolutely, 88-93% of all dated geocoded rows in those decades come from the ice (4,398 of 4,962 in the 1970s; 6,364 of 6,806 in the 1980s). 1990s-2010s: hot-desert programs catch up — by the 2000s, Antarctica's share drops to 39% (4,459 Antarctic vs 6,999 elsewhere) as Saharan, Arabian, and Atacaman searches expand.

raw_evidence.label: Background: Where Finds come from — Antarctic blue ice
raw_evidence.content: The 44,609 Finds in the dataset are wildly geographically skewed, and the reason is operational, not physical: nearly all meteorites land more or less uniformly across the planet, but they only stand out in two places — Antarctic blue ice and hot deserts. The Antarctic Search for Meteorites (ANSMET), run from Case Western Reserve University since 1976, dispatches teams of 4–10 scientists for 5–7 weeks each austral summer; they ride snowmobiles spaced 30 m apart across blue-ice areas. Blue ice forms where katabatic winds blowing off the polar plateau ablate snow faster than it falls, exposing dense, blue-tinted ice in which meteorites accumulated over hundreds of thousands of years are scoured back to the surface. As of late 2022 ANSMET alone had recovered slightly more than 23,000 specimens; combined with Japanese (NIPR) and Chinese programs, well over half of all officially-named meteorites in this snapshot are from Antarctica. None of these are Fells: the rocks have been entombed in ice for millennia.
